title: GATE CS Topic Test — Compiler Design (Set 1)
titleEn: GATE CS Topic Test — Compiler Design (Set 1)

questions.questionTextEn: When merging CLR(1) states that share the same LR(0) core to form an LALR(1) parser, which type of conflict can be newly introduced?
optionsEn: Shift-Reduce conflict only
Reduce-Reduce conflict only
Both Shift-Reduce and Reduce-Reduce conflicts
Neither — LALR(1) never introduces new conflicts
questions.explanationEn: Merging LR(1) states with identical cores never introduces a new Shift-Reduce conflict, because shift actions depend only on the core; however, combining lookahead sets of two reduce items can create a new Reduce-Reduce conflict.

questions.questionTextEn: Which three-address code representation avoids storing explicit temporary variable names by referring to results using instruction indices, making code motion harder unless an auxiliary pointer array is used?
optionsEn: Quadruples
Triples
Postfix notation
Syntax Trees
questions.explanationEn: Triples store `(op, arg1, arg2)` and reference prior results by their table index; moving an instruction changes its index and requires updating all references (which indirect triples solve).

questions.questionTextEn: Consider an `if-else` statement where variable `x` is modified in the `if` branch (`x = 1`) and also modified in the `else` branch (`x = 2`), and then printed after the `if-else` merges. How many `φ`-functions for variable `x` are inserted at the merge point in minimal SSA form?
questions.explanationEn: At the single control-flow join node immediately after the `if-else`, one `φ`-function (`x3 = φ(x1, x2)`) merges the two reaching definitions of `x`.

questions.questionTextEn: Peephole optimization is typically performed on:
optionsEn: The parse tree during syntax analysis
The symbol table
A small sliding window of target/assembly instructions
The raw source code before lexical analysis
questions.explanationEn: Peephole optimization inspects a short sequence (window) of generated target instructions to eliminate local redundancies such as redundant load/store pairs or jumps to jumps.

questions.questionTextEn: Using the Ershov / Sethi-Ullman numbering algorithm, what is the minimum number of registers required to evaluate the expression `(a + b) * (c - d)` without spilling to memory (assuming binary ops take two register operands and leaves are loaded into registers)?
questions.explanationEn: By Ershov/Sethi-Ullman numbering (both operands in registers): each leaf has label 1; both `(a + b)` and `(c - d)` have equal-label children (1, 1) so each gets label 2; the root `*` has equal-label children (2, 2), requiring 2 + 1 = 3 registers.

questions.questionTextEn: In a language supporting nested procedures and static (lexical) scoping, what is the purpose of an 'access link' (static link) in an activation record?
optionsEn: To store heap-allocated objects
To locate non-local variables declared in lexically enclosing scopes
To hold the return value of the function
To point to the caller's activation record for returning control
questions.explanationEn: The control (dynamic) link points to the caller's activation record, while the access (static) link points to the most recent activation of the lexically enclosing procedure to access non-local variables.

questions.questionTextEn:
Consider the grammar:
`S -> A B`
`A -> a | ε`
`B -> b | c`
How many symbols (including `$` if present) are in `FOLLOW(A)`?
questions.explanationEn: `A` is immediately followed by `B` in `S -> A B`. Since `ε ∉ FIRST(B) = {b, c}`, `FOLLOW(A) = FIRST(B) = {b, c}`, which has 2 symbols.

questions.questionTextEn:
Consider the grammar:
`S -> A B c`
`A -> a | ε`
`B -> b | ε`
How many terminals belong to `FIRST(S)` (do NOT count `ε` as a terminal)?
questions.explanationEn: Since `A` can derive `ε` and `B` can derive `ε`, `FIRST(S) = {a, b, c}` — 3 terminals.

questions.questionTextEn: Which of the following statements about parsers are TRUE?
optionsEn: Every ambiguous grammar fails to be LL(1) and fails to be LR(k) for any k >= 0
SLR(1) and LALR(1) parsers always have the exact same number of states for a given grammar
CLR(1) parsers generally have more states than LALR(1) parsers for the same grammar
Every LL(1) grammar is also an LR(1) grammar
questions.explanationEn: No ambiguous grammar is LL(k) or LR(k) (A); SLR(1) and LALR(1) both have the LR(0) state count (B); CLR(1) splits states by lookahead (C); and LL(1) ⊂ LR(1) (D). All four are true.

questions.questionTextEn: In a lexical analyzer generated by Flex/Lex, when two regular expression patterns match prefixes of different lengths at the current input position, which rule is applied?
optionsEn: The pattern listed last in the specification wins
A lexical error is raised immediately
Shortest match wins
Longest match (maximal munch) wins
questions.explanationEn: Lexical analyzers follow the 'maximal munch' (longest match) rule, breaking ties of equal length by preferring the pattern listed first.
Under call-by-reference, `x` binds to `&i` and `y` binds to `&a[1]` (evaluated once at call time). `t = 1`, `i = 20`, `a[1] = 1`. Thus `i = 20` and `a[1] = 1`.

questions.questionTextEn: Which of the following statements about compiler front-end and back-end design are TRUE?
optionsEn: Separating the compiler into a language-dependent front-end and a target-dependent back-end connected by a common IR allows supporting `M` languages and `N` targets with `M + N` components instead of `M × N`
Lex/Flex generates lexical analyzers based on Deterministic Finite Automata
Yacc/Bison generates LALR(1) bottom-up parsers by default
The front-end is responsible for target-specific register allocation
questions.explanationEn: A, B, and C are core compiler architecture principles. Register allocation depends on the target CPU's register set and belongs to the back-end (D is false).

questions.questionTextEn: In Reaching Definitions data-flow analysis, the data-flow equation for `OUT[B]` of a basic block `B` in terms of `IN[B]`, `GEN[B]`, and `KILL[B]` is:
optionsEn: OUT[B] = GEN[B] ∩ (IN[B] - KILL[B])
OUT[B] = (GEN[B] ∪ IN[B]) - KILL[B]
OUT[B] = GEN[B] ∪ (IN[B] - KILL[B])
OUT[B] = IN[B] ∪ (GEN[B] - KILL[B])
questions.explanationEn: Definitions generated inside `B` (`GEN[B]`) always reach the end of `B`, along with incoming definitions (`IN[B]`) that are NOT overwritten (`KILL[B]`) in `B`.

questions.questionTextEn:
Consider the augmented grammar:
`S' -> S`
`S -> a S | b`
How many states are in the canonical collection of LR(0) item sets (including the initial state `I0`)?
questions.explanationEn: The canonical LR(0) item sets are: I0 = {S'->.S, S->.aS, S->.b}, I1 = {S'->S.}, I2 = {S->a.S, S->.aS, S->.b}, I3 = {S->b.}, and I4 = {S->aS.} — 5 states in total.

questions.questionTextEn:
Consider the three-address code:
1. `a = 1`
2. `if a > 5 goto 6`
3. `b = a * 2`
4. `a = a + 1`
5. `goto 2`
6. `c = b + 1`
7. `return c`
How many edges are in the Control Flow Graph (CFG) among the basic blocks (excluding virtual ENTRY/EXIT nodes)?
questions.explanationEn: Leaders: 1, 2 (target of 5), 3 (after jump at 2), 6 (target of 2 and after jump at 5). Blocks: B1={1}, B2={2}, B3={3,4,5}, B4={6,7}. Edges: B1->B2, B2->B3 (false), B2->B4 (true), B3->B2 (goto 2). Total = 4 edges.

questions.topicTag: Compiler Design — Interference Graph Chromatic Number
questions.questionTextEn: Five variables `v1, v2, v3, v4, v5` form a 5-cycle in the live-variable interference graph (`v1-v2-v3-v4-v5-v1`, with no other edges). What is the minimum number of CPU registers needed to color this interference graph without spilling?
questions.explanationEn: An odd cycle `C_5` is not 2-colorable (chromatic number `χ(C_5) = 3`), so a minimum of 3 registers is required.

questions.questionTextEn: In a Control Flow Graph (CFG) with entry node `E`, which of the following properties of the dominance relation (`d dom n`) are ALWAYS TRUE?
optionsEn: If `a dom b` and `b dom c`, then `a dom c` (transitive)
The entry node `E` dominates every reachable node in the CFG
Every node other than `E` has a unique immediate dominator (idom)
Every node dominates itself (reflexive)
questions.explanationEn: Dominance is a partial order rooted at `E` forming a dominator tree, so reflexivity, transitivity, entry dominance, and unique immediate dominators all hold.

questions.questionTextEn: Moving a statement `x = y + z` out of a `for` loop to a preheader block (when neither `y` nor `z` is modified inside the loop) is called:
optionsEn: Induction variable elimination
Loop-invariant code motion (code hoisting)
Loop unrolling
Loop interchange
questions.explanationEn: Loop-invariant code motion hoists computations whose operands do not change inside the loop to the loop preheader so they execute once instead of on every iteration.

questions.questionTextEn: In Live Variable Analysis, for a basic block `B` with `USE[B]` (variables used before any definition in `B`) and `DEF[B]` (variables defined before any use in `B`), the backward equations are:
optionsEn: OUT[B] = ∪_{S ∈ succ(B)} IN[S],  IN[B] = DEF[B] ∪ (OUT[B] - USE[B])
OUT[B] = ∪_{S ∈ succ(B)} IN[S],  IN[B] = USE[B] ∪ (OUT[B] - DEF[B])
IN[B] = ∪_{P ∈ pred(B)} OUT[P],  OUT[B] = USE[B] ∪ (IN[B] - DEF[B])
OUT[B] = ∩_{S ∈ succ(B)} IN[S],  IN[B] = USE[B] ∪ (OUT[B] - DEF[B])
questions.explanationEn: A variable is live at the exit of `B` (`OUT[B]`) if it is live at the entry of *any* successor `S`. It is live at the entry of `B` (`IN[B]`) if it is used in `B` before definition (`USE[B]`) or live at exit and not killed by `DEF[B]`.
